{{short description|Converse to Pascal's theorem In geometry}}
[[File:Braikenridge–Maclaurin theorem.svg|thumb|Elliptic case]]
[[File:Braikenridge–Maclaurin theorem 2.svg|thumb|Hyperbolic case]]
In [[geometry]], the '''{{visible anchor|Braikenridge–Maclaurin theorem}}''', named for 18th-century British mathematicians [[William Braikenridge]] and [[Colin Maclaurin]],{{r|mills}} is the converse to [[Pascal's theorem]].  It states that if the three intersection points of the three pairs of lines through opposite sides of a hexagon lie on a line ''L'', then the six vertices of the hexagon lie on a conic ''C''; the conic may be degenerate, as in [[Pappus's hexagon theorem]].{{r|cg}}

The Braikenridge–Maclaurin theorem may be applied in the [[Braikenridge–Maclaurin construction]], which is a [[synthetic geometry|synthetic]] construction of the conic defined by five points, by varying the sixth point.  Namely, Pascal's theorem states that given six points on a conic (the vertices of a hexagon), the lines defined by opposite sides intersect in three collinear points. This can be reversed to construct the possible locations for a sixth point, given five existing ones.
